title: Spanish Tortilla
kicker: Three ingredients — egg, potato, olive oil — and the most argued-about technique in Spain.
story: Tortilla de patatas is Spain's dish of the people: a thick potato omelet, golden outside and barely-set inside, cut in wedges and eaten at any hour. Every bar has one, every family has an opinion about the interior — juicy (jugosa) versus fully set — and the arguments have real geopolitical energy.

The traditional technique feels extravagant until you try it: potatoes poached in generous olive oil rather than fried hard, so they turn buttery-soft without color. That oil, infused with potato, is strained and reused — it becomes liquid gold for the next tortilla. Some add onion; Spain divides itself over this ('con cebolla' vs 'sin cebolla') with the fervor of a national election. This recipe says yes, onion, and dares you to complain.
fun_fact: Legend places the invention in the 1830s Carlist Wars, where a Basque general was served it by a farmhouse family. First written mention is 1817, scolding Navarran convents for eating eggs and potatoes in omelets while the poor starved.

ingredients.note: Yukon gold or similar, sliced 5 mm
the better the egg, the better the tortilla
not extra-virgin's expensive cousin; regular olive oil

steps.title: Poach in oil
steps.text: Warm the oil in a small deep pan over medium-low. Add potato slices and onion; they should barely bubble. Cook 20-25 minutes, occasionally nudging, until potatoes are tender enough to break with a spoon — no browning.

steps.title: Strain the liquid gold
steps.text: Drain, reserving the oil. It now tastes of potato; it will make your next tortilla, or this one's flip, measurably better.

steps.title: Rest the mixture
steps.text: Beat eggs with a big pinch of salt, fold in warm potatoes gently, and rest 10 minutes. The potatoes drink egg and the whole thing coheres better in the pan.

steps.title: The first side
steps.text: Wipe out the pan, film it with the reserved oil, get it properly hot. Pour the mixture. Cook 3 minutes on medium-high, then lower and cook 4-5 more until the bottom is set and golden. The center should still wobble.

steps.title: The flip
steps.text: Slide a plate over the pan, flip in one committed motion, slide the tortilla back in raw-side down. Cook 3-4 minutes. Two plates are safer than one; commitment matters more than equipment.

steps.title: Rest before slicing
steps.text: Tortilla is best warm or room temperature, never hot — the custard sets as it rests. Wedge it, and eat it as breakfast, lunch, tapa, or midnight snack. It declines no occasions.

notes: The interior should still be soft — a tortilla cooked dry all the way through is a different, sadder food.
Reserved potato oil keeps in the fridge for a month and upgrades everything fried in it.
Individual tortillas (small, quick, 4 cm tall) are a legit Spanish street food — same recipe, smaller pan, bolder flip.

storage: Refrigerates 3 days; traditional Spanish bars leave it at room temperature all day, but home food-safety says chill it. Best eaten at room temperature — take it out 30 minutes before serving.

equipment.n: nonstick or well-seasoned, 20-22 cm - the flip needs a plate larger than the pan and one deep breath
potatoes at 3 mm, even; or a very calm knife

facts.origin: Spain — Basque Country and Navarra both claim it
facts.first_recorded: First written mention 1817; the Carlist-general legends are later decorations
facts.name_means: Tortilla here means 'little cake' — nothing to do with the Mexican kind, a fact learned by everyone once, awkwardly.
facts.technique: Low-slow potato confit, then the flip (one plate, one breath)
facts.season: Any — it is lunch, dinner and midnight alike
facts.signature: Silky potato interior, jammy center, olive oil richness
facts.serve_at: Room temperature — which is its superpower
facts.pour: Albariño, or nothing — tortilla travels alone

similar.n: Mediterranean patience, best at room temperature
Spanish pan logic: shallow, confident, shared from the vessel
